questions.problem: Determine the horizontal asymptote of the function $f(x)=\frac{2x({x}^{3}+1)}{3{x}^{4}-7}.$
questions.worked_solution:
The given function can be rewritten as follows:

$$
f(x)=\frac{2{x}^{4}+2x}{3{x}^{4}-7}
$$

To find the horizontal asymptote of a rational function, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by the dominant term in the denominator, and then we let $x\to \infty .$

Ignoring the coefficient, the dominant term in the denominator is ${x}^{4}.$ So, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by ${x}^{4},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{2{x}^{4}+2x}{3{x}^{4}-7} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{2{x}^{4}}{{x}^{4}}+\frac{2x}{{x}^{4}})}{(\frac{3{x}^{4}}{{x}^{4}}-\frac{7}{{x}^{4}})} \\  & =\frac{(2+\frac{2}{{x}^{3}})}{(3-\frac{7}{{x}^{4}})}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, when $x$ is very large, the terms $\frac{2}{{x}^{3}}$ and $\frac{7}{{x}^{4}}$ become very small. Therefore, as $x\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{(2+\frac{2}{{x}^{3}})}{(3-\frac{7}{{x}^{4}})} \\  & \to \frac{2+0}{3-0} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

So, the horizontal asymptote is $y=\frac{2}{3}.$

questions.problem: The horizontal asymptote of the function $f(x)=\frac{4{x}^{3}-5{x}^{2}+3}{2-{x}^{3}}$ is $y=${{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
To find the horizontal asymptote of a rational function, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by the dominant term in the denominator, and then we let $x\to \infty .$

In this case, the dominant term in the denominator is ${x}^{3}.$ So, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by ${x}^{3},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{4{x}^{3}-5{x}^{2}+3}{2-{x}^{3}} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{4{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}}-\frac{5{x}^{2}}{{x}^{3}}+\frac{3}{{x}^{3}})}{(\frac{2}{{x}^{3}}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}})} \\  & =\frac{(4-\frac{5}{x}+\frac{3}{{x}^{3}})}{(\frac{2}{{x}^{3}}-1)}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, when $x$ is very large, the terms $\frac{5}{x},$ $\frac{3}{{x}^{3}},$ and $\frac{2}{{x}^{3}}$ become very small. Therefore, as $x\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{(4-\frac{5}{x}+\frac{3}{{x}^{3}})}{(\frac{2}{{x}^{3}}-1)} \\  & \to \frac{4-0+0}{0-1} \\  & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the horizontal asymptote is $y=-4.$

questions.problem: The horizontal asymptote of the function $f(x)=\frac{8{x}^{4}+6x}{({x}^{2}-2x)(1-2{x}^{2})}$ is $y=${{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
The given function can be rewritten as follows:

$$
f(x)=\frac{8{x}^{4}-6x}{-2{x}^{4}+4{x}^{3}+{x}^{2}-2x}
$$

To find the horizontal asymptote of a rational function, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by the dominant term in the denominator, and then we let $x\to \infty .$

Ignoring the coefficient, the dominant term in the denominator is ${x}^{4}.$ So, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by ${x}^{4},$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{8{x}^{4}-6x}{-2{x}^{4}+4{x}^{3}+{x}^{2}-2x} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{8{x}^{4}}{{x}^{4}}-\frac{6x}{{x}^{4}})}{(-\frac{2{x}^{4}}{{x}^{4}}+\frac{4{x}^{3}}{{x}^{4}}+\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{4}}-\frac{2x}{{x}^{4}})} \\  & =\frac{(8-\frac{6}{{x}^{3}})}{(-2+\frac{4}{x}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}-\frac{2}{{x}^{3}})}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, when $x$ is very large, the terms $\frac{6}{{x}^{3}},$ $\frac{4}{x},$ $\frac{1}{{x}^{2}},$ and $\frac{2}{{x}^{3}}$ become very small. Therefore, as $x\to \infty ,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{(8-\frac{6}{{x}^{3}})}{(-2+\frac{4}{x}+\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}-\frac{2}{{x}^{3}})} \\  & \to \frac{8-0}{-2+0+0-0} \\  & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the horizontal asymptote is $y=-4.$

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{3+4{x}^{2}-2{x}^{3}}{{x}^{2}-x} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{3}{{x}^{2}}+\frac{4{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}-\frac{2{x}^{3}}{{x}^{2}})}{(\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}-\frac{x}{{x}^{2}})} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{3}{{x}^{2}}+4-2x)}{(1-\frac{1}{x})}\end{aligned}

canonical_examples.problem: Determine the horizontal asymptote of the function $f(x) = \dfrac{4x^3-x}{3x^3+24}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
To find the horizontal asymptote of a rational function, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by the dominant term in the denominator, and then we let $x\to\infty.$

Ignoring the coefficient, the dominant term in the denominator is $x^3.$ So, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by $x^3,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{4{x}^{3}-x}{3{x}^{3}+24} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{4{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}}-\frac{x}{{x}^{3}})}{(\frac{3{x}^{3}}{{x}^{3}}+\frac{24}{{x}^{3}})} \\  & =\frac{(4-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})}{(3+\frac{24}{{x}^{3}})}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, when $x$ is very large, the terms $\dfrac{1}{x^2}$ and $\dfrac{24}{x^3}$ become very small. Therefore, as $x\to\infty,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{(4-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})}{(3+\frac{24}{{x}^{3}})} \\  & \to \frac{4-0}{3+0} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, the horizontal asymptote is $y = \dfrac{4}{3}.$

Ignoring the coefficient, the dominant term in the denominator is $x^2.$ So, we divide every term in the numerator and denominator by $x^2,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{2{x}^{3}}{{x}^{2}-1} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{2{x}^{3}}{{x}^{2}})}{(\frac{{x}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})} \\  & =\frac{2x}{(1-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, when $x$ is very large, the term $\dfrac{1}{x^2}$ becomes very small. Therefore, as $x\to\infty,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x) & =\frac{2x}{(1-\frac{1}{{x}^{2}})} \\  & ≈\frac{2x}{1-0} \\  & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

This is not a constant, which means that $y = f(x)$ does not have a horizontal asymptote.
